findings.title: Subdomain policy weaker than parent policy
findings.detail: Subdomain policy is set to "none" while parent policy is "reject". This leaves subdomains vulnerable to spoofing.

findings.title: Non-existent subdomains spoofable (np=none)
findings.detail: The organizational domain enforces DMARC but non-existent subdomains resolve to np=none, leaving them spoofable (e.g. payroll.example.com). Set np=reject to close this gap.

findings.title: Third-party DMARC aggregator detected
findings.detail: Using third-party aggregator(s): powerdmarc.com. Ensure these services are authorized to receive your DMARC reports.

findings.title: No forensic reporting configured (ruf= absent)
findings.detail: Aggregate reporting (rua=) is configured but forensic reporting (ruf=) is not. Forensic reports provide detailed failure information useful for troubleshooting.

findings.title: Relaxed DKIM alignment
findings.detail: DKIM alignment mode is relaxed (adkim=r or unset). Consider adkim=s (strict) for stronger authentication.

findings.title: Relaxed SPF alignment
findings.detail: SPF alignment mode is relaxed (aspf=r or unset). Strict alignment (aspf=s) only strengthens DMARC when every authorized sender's return-path (envelope-from) domain exactly matches the From domain — untrue for most ESP-relayed mail (e.g. Resend, SendGrid, Mailchimp, SES with a custom MAIL FROM), where the return-path sits on a subdomain: wherever the From domain differs from it (typically the apex), aspf=s fails SPF alignment for that traffic and leaves DKIM as the only authentication leg. Mail whose From address stays on that same subdomain still aligns under aspf=s. Set aspf=s only after DMARC aggregate reports confirm every sender's return-path domain exactly matches the From domain; otherwise aspf=r is the correct setting.

findings.title: TXT RRset exceeds UDP limit
findings.detail: The combined TXT RRset for health.govt.nz is ~707 bytes, which exceeds the 512-byte UDP limit and requires TCP fallback. Legacy resolvers and restrictive middleboxes that do not retry over TCP may only see the first ~512 bytes, silently breaking SPF for some receiving MTAs. RFC 7208 §3.4 advises keeping the SPF record and surrounding TXT RRset small enough to fit a single UDP packet.

findings.title: SPF delegates to shared sending platform (unrecognized): _spf.createsend.com
findings.detail: SPF include:_spf.createsend.com delegates sending to an external multi-tenant-style platform that is not in the recognized ESP catalog. It still widens your trust surface even though the specific provider is not named. This is common and not inherently a misconfiguration, but it expands the sending infrastructure you rely on. The risk becomes more material when DMARC enforcement and alignment are weak.

findings.title: SPF delegates to shared platform: Microsoft 365
findings.detail: SPF include:spf.protection.outlook.com authorizes Microsoft 365. Any M365 tenant can send as your domain without DKIM/DMARC enforcement. This is common and not inherently a misconfiguration, but it expands the sending infrastructure you rely on. The risk becomes more material when DMARC enforcement and alignment are weak.

findings.title: SPF trust surface: 3 shared platforms
findings.detail: SPF record delegates sending authority to 3 multi-tenant platforms (_spf.createsend.com (unrecognized), spf.odmad.quest-on-demand.com (unrecognized), Microsoft 365). Audit each include to confirm it is still needed, configure provider-specific DKIM, and keep DMARC enforcement and alignment strong across every authorized sender.
